utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Schou, good afternoon. I would like to pick up now where we left off on Friday. Mr. Schou, you told us that you spent the night between the 19th and the 20th at Negoslavci. On the morning of the 20th the meeting was held at the JNA headquarters, at least if all the reports we have seen are to be believed. Do you know who exactly attended the meeting on the morning of the 20th at the JNA headquarters in Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have Exhibit 320 placed on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This is at tab 22 for you, Mr. Schou. Sir, if you look at this report, can you see what the teams were on the 20th, and which persons did that team comprise?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find the paper. You said 22?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Tab 22. This is page 1. I think it must be the one you're looking at. The team on the 20th of November. It's right at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. November the 20th, Cunningham, Kanteres, Schou, and Kypr are the members of the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If we look at this report it seems that Mr. Pavkovic chaired the meeting, didn't he? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I just remember there was a colonel on that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If you look at the portion of the report that reads, "Contact and names." You will see that at number 1 we have Colonel Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Could this be the same colonel who chaired the meeting, the one that you saw at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, do you remember what exactly you were informed about at the meeting involving the wounded who were at the time in the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only remember that some -- that some in the hospital were arrested during the night. I don't -- do not remember any more about that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Schou, if you look at the portion of the report under the heading, "Main points" that's on page 2 of the written report. If you could look at paragraph 3 of the report. You will read it out to you and, please confirm if my reading is accurate. "A short briefing with 1." 1, meaning Colonel Pavkovic, as we established a moment ago, it says, "Wounded members of the Croatian paramilitary forces must remain here. They later told us that those members had been captured and that they had left the hospital before our arrival as well as certain members of the former staff, Dr. Bosanac." Does this tally with what you told us a while ago, that you were informed that some people had been taken away from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't find the page in the paper, but I just --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I will help you with that, sir. This is page 3 -- I'm sorry, page 2 of the handwritten report.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that, sir? That this is indeed what was discussed at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as I told you before, I just remember that some of the -- some of the patients and some of the staff were arrested before we arrived in hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. What I want to know is, is this what Colonel Pavkovic told you? The person who chaired the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact -- exactly which person who said this one, but -- I can't remember exact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember when you left the meeting in Negoslavci, were you held up in Vukovar for about two hours, and why?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were held up in -- at the bridge in Vukovar for about two hours, and it -- the reason was that it was for our secure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Was the reason that you were not save the fact that some of the streets that you were supposed to take were booby-trapped?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that question, how can this witness know if he was held up? There's a difference between something being said and the truth of what it is. The question is asking for confirmation of the truth, not the fact it's said. There is a difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You followed that, have you, Mr. Bulatovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. No problem at all. I will rephrase my question altogether. It will be clear then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you know what the reason was for you being detained there, what was it that put your personal safety at risk?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told that there were snipers and that there still were some mines on the roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If you look at the report in front of you, do you remember there being any references to snipers in that report, sir?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If you look at page 3, that's the B/C/S reference, and your reference is page 2, the handwritten portion under "c)." it says "Vukovar." Have you found that, Mr. Schou?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: "Vukovar: Two hours wait in the centre of town. Mines being cleared." Can we then agree that there is no reference to any snipers in this official report?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no reference there, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember how long it took you from Negoslavci to reach the bridge where you were stopped?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact time, but the -- the kilometre is just five to 10, so it couldn't take long time. But I can't remember the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If you bear in mind the schedule contained in that report, and all your commitments on the 20th of November, it says departure for Vukovar at 8.45. You said at about 8.00. I will allow for this small discrepancy. What was the time or what could have been the time by the time you reached that bridge where you were stopped, roughly speaking?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the time exactly, but I remember we arrived the bridge, and then we were waiting there for about two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When you reached the bridge, did you see Mr. Sljivancanin there immediately on your arrival?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember if it were immediately or -- he arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: While travelling along the Negoslavci-Vukovar road, did you come across any other JNA officers driving, walking, regardless?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: We listed the members of your team a while ago. Were you driving in just one vehicle, or was this a convoy containing several vehicles?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just remember that we were driving in our own vehicle, and that we have some military police in front and in back when we drive this road.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Was your JNA liaison officer with you at this time?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the reason for his absence?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When you reached the bridge was Mr. Borsinger already there?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think I remember that he arrived later.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember how much later, exactly?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about the discussion between Mr. Borsinger and Mr. Sljivancanin at the bridge. Did you see Mr. Borsinger involved in a debate with any other JNA officers there?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I think we looked at Mr. Cunningham's report, it's at tab 27 in your binder, sir. Can you please find that for me? Can we please have Exhibit 333 displayed on our screens? Mr. Schou, as I said, for your convenience, tab 27. Have you found that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the top say 4269 or something like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: 4267, that's the page number for you, sir. If you could look at item 7, please. I will read it out. In the English this is ZA00-4267. Item 7. The Behaviour of the ICRC Leader: Evacuation in Vukovar. "The representative of the ICRC first caught my eye at Negoslavci when I saw him and Colonel M, our JNA liaison officer, engaged in a heated debate about something. Several hours later the ICRC representative suddenly joined the meeting that I was having with Colonel Pavkovic, the purpose of which was to tackle all the issues from the message that had been faxed about the evacuation of the Vukovar Hospital. I explained that he was responsible for taking these steps under item 6 of the fax, as well as for compiling and keeping detailed lists of everyone leaving the hospital. He failed to provide an explanation and just left the meeting. The next time I saw him was right in the middle of Vukovar engaged in a shouting match and an argument with Colonel Pavkovic." Mr. Schou, this is Mr. Cunningham's report. Do you remember this argument or altercation between the ICRC representative and Colonel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Were you there when Mr. Borsinger was having an argument with Mr. Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: How far were you standing from them?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 20 metre.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: We heard a while ago that Mr. Pavkovic, at least that's what you seem to remember, and also based on the report that we looked at a while ago, it appears that Mr. Pavkovic was chairing the meeting in Negoslavci. Do you remember this colonel, Mr. Pavkovic, from Negoslavci? Did you see him at the bridge?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him at the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see him engaging in any sort of contact with the ICRC representative?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I told you before, I don't remember any contact between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we please play the video that is Exhibit 335? That is a video clip we have a transcript, which has been marked for identification. If the technicians could please play that video clip. And the transcript is 336, if Mr. Schou could please have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Schou, you had the transcript of this conversation in front of you. The dialogue is partly in English. Based on this, can we conclude that Colonel Pavkovic did have an argument with Mr. Borsinger? Do you remember this happening?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I told you, I can't remember it happened, but -- but I were there, and you could see me on the picture. I was 20 metre behind the car. But I can't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So the footage is authentic, it shows the day when you were at the bridge, the 20th of November, 1991, and this happened in Vukovar, right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree on this, sir, having watched the footage, having heard the dialogue that took place, the JNA does not seem to be impeding the ICRC man from going to the hospital, all they're asking him to do is to move along together with the column in a vehicle in which you were too all they're asking him to do is to move his vehicle and join the column just behind your own vehicle. Isn't what you heard now?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard this, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember Mr. Cunningham being there?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If you are saying that he wasn't there, can you explain how he possibly could have been in a position to write a report such as the one that I read out to you a while ago, covering, among other things, the actions of an ICRC representative, and this report appears to be based on his personal observations?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't explain how Cunningham is saying so, but I think he must have talked with Mr. Kypr or something like that. But he wasn't -- he wasn't at that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Schou, is it possible that Mr. Cunningham was there after all, but after this he left for Belgrade immediately? Is that a possibility?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: How then can we explain the fact that I mentioned a moment ago, he is writing this report from his own perspective, he is covering the evacuation of the hospital and the steps being taken by the ICRC. How can he possibly do this if he wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The witness has already answered that particular question. I can see no point at all, and why this witness is being asked to reply to the question a second time, which is speculative in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you have made your point, Mr. Bulatovic. You can happily move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Schou, when did you reach the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact time, but it was about two hours after we arrived to -- into the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When did you enter the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I entered the hospital when we arrived to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how long you stayed in the hospital and what you did while you were inside the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stay in the hospital for about three hours, I think. I have -- I have not the exact time. But -- and I was walking around in the hospital and I had a military police person, you can say, guarding me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: During that period of time, during those three hours, did you ever go outside of the building, or were you in the building the whole time?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was also outside the building, I was outside where they were loading all the wounded in the ambulance, in the military ambulance, and I was also in the front of the building talking with one of the staff members, a lady doctor, which I was talking with one month before. But I can't remember what we were talking about. She was just saying a few things.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Schou, can you please tell me, out of those three hours that you spent in the hospital how long were you outside of the building when you talked to this person outside of the building, when you observed the wounded being loaded on to ambulances?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact time I was outside the building and how long time I stay in the building. I was just walking around that three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Borsinger in front of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Schou, if I were to tell you that we had witnesses here during the trial who confirmed that on the 20th in the morning they saw Mr. Borsinger in front of the hospital and that they saw him talking to Mr. Sljivancanin, would you say that it was possible that he was, after all, in front of the hospital at the time when you were inside the building and that that was the reason why you did not see him?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't -- that's -- of course it is possible, but I -- I did not see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On Friday when answering questions put to you by Mr. Borovic, you said that your personal opinion was that Mr. Borsinger could have done more; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Could we now show Exhibit 333, tab 27, please. We had that document on the screen just a little bit ago. Let us just see it again to remind us of its content. Let us now see the portion from item 7, which concerns the conduct of the International Committee of the Red Cross leaders. We read this out, Mr. Schou, just about 10 minutes ago. Let me ask you this: Can we agree that based on this report that I read out to you just a little bit ago, this item 7 concerning the conduct of the ICRC representatives, this is your report that was submitted, and in addition to that we also saw on Friday the report that you saw. And, based on that, can we agree that the reason for the inadequate work of Mr. Borsinger and the ICRC did not come about because their work was hindered by the JNA, and you could see that based on the video showing his conversation with Mr. Pavkovic, but rather that the reason for their inadequate work was that Mr. Borsinger was a man, who in your words, did not do anything, who came into conflict with your liaison officer, Mr. Memisevic, who also had a clash with chief of mission, Mr. Cunningham, who was also the team leader. He had a clash with Mr. Sljivancanin, and Mr. Pavkovic. Therefore, this is a conflict-prone personality, that of Mr. Borsinger. Could we conclude that, based on all of these facts that I just cited to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I object to the question, if it is a question. It's more a statement, in my submission. The question is perfectly simple, I would have thought. And that is whether in actual fact, as has been declared, allegedly, whether the ICRC representative was unable to proceed, that the inadequacy was his and not as a result of the JNA blocking him. Surely that is the question that has to be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, please, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wanted to hear the position of the witness based on all of the evidence, reports of the mission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to see witness's position concerning Mr. Borsinger.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Schou, can you answer my question, please?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I can say to that is to my opinion Mr. Borsinger was not good for his job, and some things were because he were in conflict with everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Schou, I'd like to go back to a date that I should have addressed first, but due to the relevance of other questions, I turned to them first. I would like now to discuss the convoy of the 9th of October in which you participated.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's question, 19th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Was Mr. Michele [phoen] in that convoy? This is the gentleman who was a representative of Medecins sans Frontieres. I think that you mentioned him and said that you knew him.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him. He is an ECMM member, he is not a representative of Medecins sans Frontieres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The information I have indicates otherwise, but perhaps it's possible what you are saying. Was he in the convoy on the 19th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am a little confused. Mr. Michele, can you describe him for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Schou, I was about to ask you to describe him for us.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- the leader of our convoy was a French colonel, and I think his name was something like that, but I'm not sure I can recognise him on the photo. We had the photo on Friday where he was drinking, I think the sljivovic with Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we now see Exhibit 338, photograph 1? Which is 0036-6974. This is the number of the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see it on the screen, the photograph, Mr. Schou?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you take this photograph?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think this photograph is taken -- taken one month before I arrived in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The man you see in this photograph, is this Mr. Robert Michele, based on your recollection?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know perhaps where this photograph was taken and on which occasion?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I just remember that it was taken in a JNA barracks somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: As for convoy on the 19th of October, 1991, do you remember who said that the convoy should take the route via Marinci, Luzac, and Vukovar -- Vukovar barracks?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have a correction for the transcript, page 14, line 9. Bogdanovci is missing from the route taken. It should be Marinci, Bogdanovci, Luzac, and Vukovar Hospital. Not the barracks, but rather the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who provided guarantees to the chief of the convoy that this route was safe?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that before the convoy entered Vukovar on the 19th of October you were stopped in the village of Marinci?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just have to look at a map to see how -- which really is Marinci. I just have to find the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Could we see a sketch on the screen, please? ERN number 0036-6971. This sketch has not been admitted into evidence yet, but I believe it will be of assistance to the witness if he were to see it on the screen. If it's a problem to put it on the screen, Your Honours, I have a hard copy of it and I can provide it to the witness if the usher will help me so that we do not waste any more time.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have my own. Yes, we were stopped in Marinci for, I think, half an hour or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether Mr. Pavkovic and Mr. Sljivancanin were there?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that on that occasion it was suggested to you that when travelling to Vukovar you should travel via Marinci, Petrovci, Vukovar, and that you rejected this suggestion?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that the JNA representatives who stopped you in Marinci told you that Bogdanovci was under the control of the Croatian forces, the so-called Croatian army, and that the area around Bogdanovci had been mined, therefore they were unable to guarantee your safety there?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether Croatian forces indeed had Bogdanovci under their control at the time?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember when we arrived Bogdanovci, there was Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: As a man who has military training and holds a military rank, let me ask you this: If certain forces have a certain place under their control, is it then a fact that these forces placed the mines around that location in order to defend themselves? In other words, are the mines usually placed by those who are defending the area, or those who are attacking it, based on your experience?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's placed by the forces who are defending -- defending their area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The positions protected in this manner, were they also safe-guarded by some other military means? You will agree with me that mines alone do not mean much unless there are other sorts of protection.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only talk about my own military experience. Mines alone are not -- are nothing, but you have to guard them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember whether this route that I just read out to you, Marinci, Petrovci, Bogdanovci, Vukovar Hospital, was the JNA informed of this route when you set out from Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And we have a liaison officer with us from the military -- from the military headquarter in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The ones who were leading the convoy who escaped, as you said, upon seeing a tank, who were these people, if you know?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only saw them, and they were -- they wearing military uniforms of that kind like -- yes, soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of uniforms? Uniforms of which army?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. After a vehicle hit a mine, the incident that you described to us, you said that after that on that day you did not speak to Mr. Sljivancanin, you were stopped by a tank, and then you told us that you did not speak to Mr. Sljivancanin, but that however you heard that he had told somebody, perhaps the chief of mission, that you need to turn back. Do you remember this conversation?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only -- only remember that -- when I heard that we should take the -- the agreed road back.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that the chief of your mission, or perhaps the leader of the convoy, asked the JNA to take him to the road to Bogdanovci, that that was the only request put forward?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that evening, after the incident with the mine when the army took you to the road to Petrovci, how long did it take to pull your convoy out of that area and to the other area and under what circumstances did that take place?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember we get stuck in the fields, and that we get help from the APC, from the Yugoslavian forces to reach a normal road, and I think it take one hour or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So the whole process to pull the convoy out took one hour; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my opinion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Schou, let me ask you something else. Before you were sent to the area as a member of the ECMM, did you have any information and, if so, what type of information, concerning the nature and type of the conflict taking place in the territory of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we get a briefing in our intelligence headquarter in Denmark where they told us about Yugoslavia and the conflict and which kind of people in each region, and what they -- what they were working, how they speak, which kind of language, which church they believe, and all this thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did they tell you anything about the ethnic composition of the population in the area to which you were sent?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what you were told about the ethnic composition?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told that some of the area, they were mixed by Croatian, Serbian, Bosnian, and all kind of religion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did they tell you why an armed conflict erupted? What kind of explanation did they give you for that?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: They only tell us that some part of the country want to be -- to be separate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember which part of the country it was which wanted to secede?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the word "secede."

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: To secede means to leave some kind of a union, to break away from it.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, we were told that Slovenian was trying to secede, and that Croatian were trying to secede.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Schou, we were able to see in your personal reports as well as in team reports that were sent to the headquarters in Zagreb, and we now need to ask you whether the Kingdom of Denmark, back in 1991, was a member of the Council of Europe?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The reports that you sent, did they ever serve as a basis for adopting certain political decisions in the Council of Europe, were they housed as material based on which the Council of Europe adopted certain decisions concerning the situation in the territory of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In my submission, the witness couldn't possibly answer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. Moore. And, Mr. Bulatovic, if you remember, we were asking you to focus on what's important to this indictment. And these are, at best, general background questions. Time is running out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have a couple of questions left and then I will conclude my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Schou, having talked to Mr. Sljivancanin, you described him as a person who made lots of political references in his conversations with you, right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When asked by my learned friend, Mr. Borovic, you said that you had heard such terms as, "Chetniks" and "Ustashas" being used without knowing exactly what those terms meant, right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the beginning I did not know what this word refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In your conversations with Mr. Sljivancanin do you remember him saying that the JNA was the only regular army around? Do you remember him referring to that fact?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that he mentioned while talking to you that all paramilitary and irregular police units should be disarmed?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember him saying, and it appears that you don't, at least not directly in your conversations, that the JNA would cease all combat operations and that they would make sure that everyone, irrespective of their ethnic background, would have the right conditions in place to have a normal life?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember that before you were dispatched to the former Yugoslavia you attended a number of briefings where you were told about the ethnic make-up of the area? Did they tell you anything about the JNA and the ethnic make-up of the JNA itself?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they tell -- yeah, tell us that the JNA was an army which contain all part of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Schou, back in 1991 did you have an opportunity to see the Yugoslav flag? Do you know what it looked like?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if that flag, which you don't remember, had a red five-pointed star on it?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember Mr. Sljivancanin telling you anything about any of the republics, or anything, or was it the case that he kept talking about the pro-Yugoslav orientation of the JNA? Do you remember anything like that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You testified that when you saw Mr. Sljivancanin on the 20th of November, 1991, you did not notice any ranks visibly displayed or any insignia. Was that the case, sir?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't -- the answer is that I -- when I saw him on the 20th November, I can't remember any rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Schou, do you remember that on the 20th of November you saw the Yugoslav flag displayed on the left-hand pocket of Mr. Sljivancanin's shirt, the Yugoslav flag, a five-pointed star? Does any of that ring a bell, sir?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bulatovic. Could I mention for all counsel that Mr. Bulatovic was concerned at one point that a sketch didn't come up quickly on the e-court. That sketch, I am told, is not in your Defence folder. Unless it's in your Defence folder, the court officials can't bring it up quickly. If you would all bear that in mind. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You have told us about a photograph showing Major Sljivancanin and gentleman called Michele sharing a glass of wine, or sljivovic, as it's been called. Do you remember that photograph?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's our Exhibit 338. You have told us that it was at a JNA barracks.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. About one month after you had arrived -- well, I'm quoting you on your evidence -- well, one month --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, the witness clearly said that the photograph was taken one month before he arrived, and not after he arrived, as Mr. Moore has just been telling us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And your date of arrival, I think you left Denmark on the 15th of October; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And we have heard evidence in relation to the 18th and 19th of October. In respect of the mission to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, can I deal with that photograph that was one month prior to your arrival? And thank you very much for that assistance. The JNA barracks, do you know where that barracks was where he met Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told at that time, but I can't remember the barracks, which name it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can you remember the location?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was in the Vukovar area, but which barracks, I'm not -- I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, indeed. Can I move on, please, to a question that you were asked, and the reply that you gave was as follows: "The only thing that I can say that Mr. Borsinger was not good for his job, and some things" - my emphasis - "was because he was in conflict with everyone." Would you look, please, I think it is our Exhibit 341, tab 40. Now, do you have tab 40 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just to remind us, it's right to say that this particular document, as we can see on the second page, was compiled by yourself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I just want to deal with one or two aspects, where you say that he was on some things were because he were in conflict with everyone. Can we deal then please, with your analysis or your conclusions in relation to your dealings with Borsinger? Now, let's go to page 1, please. Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We have got "comments." Have you got "comments" down at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And we have got then the 20th of the 11th. Have you got that entry?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, can we deal then, please, with the subheadings that you have created. ICMM was held back. Chetniks in hospital, and then there is reference, "too less ambulances and buses. Nothing prepared by JNA and ICRC." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, let's move on to A. With regard to the ICRC, it says, "Leader ICRC only criticised JNA"?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: "2: Make no list of wounded," and "do nothing"?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's deal, please, with the situation as you perceived it on the 20th for the JNA participation on that day. Could you just read it out slowly, please?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the JNA point 1, "No security, many Chetniks."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: When you say "no security," no security where?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that we were --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that the line of questioning being pursued by my learned friend right now does not arise from the cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bulatovic, I think it does. Carry on, please, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we carry on? With regard to, "No security, many Chetniks." Security in relation to what, please?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In relation to our own situation and in relation to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And when we talk about the hospital situation, can you please, in shortened form, tell us what you mean by that, the absence of security and the participation of Chetniks at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was because we saw Chetniks walking around in the hospital with weapons and beating the -- some of the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go to number 2. Have you got that?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "Too many officers. Only few soldiers."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what was the relevance of that when we talk about the JNA participation or control?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the hospital and it was almost medical staff officers I saw, and they were only few soldiers, so there were nothing to -- no people to help carrying the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's deal with number 3. "No control, no organising." What is meant by that, please in the JNA participation?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means that they were not ambulance enough, and there were no -- no system over the evacuation, no priority. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Number 4 we've already dealt with, it's subsumed within 2. 5, perhaps, is subsumed within 1. And then 6 we've got shooting in the air. And what was number 7?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 7 is, "Mortar firing from the city."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's -- that's the 20th. And you've said that the ICRC make no list of wounded. Let's turn over the page, please, to the 21st, the following day. Let's look at your view on the ICRC again, and then compare it with the JNA. So ICRC, please?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: They got good prepared, they make lists. They were -- number 2, they had good helping in organising everything but their leader only make trouble.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. So on the 20th, there is no list; on the 21st, there is a list. But you maintain your position with regard to the leader. What about the JNA? Can we deal with number 1, please?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, number 1, "Lieutenant Colonel make good job," I can't remember exactly which person it was at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Number 2, "buses bad for wounded people." Now, why are buses bad for wounded people?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they had to sit up in a bus, they were trying to put the patient on -- what do you call that, where you carry the wound.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Stretcher?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stretcher and then put it up on the back of the seat on the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And is that a good thing or a bad thing?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a bad thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Why is that a bad thing, doctor?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because when you were laying there, you are falling down when you are moving the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Let's move on then please to number 3. Better security?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Better security but still Chetniks in the hospital."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And what is meant by that on the 21st?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that there were more, you can say normal military hospital personnel in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Number 4 in some ways we've heard. And then number 5, please?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: "No security of the convoy."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And then finally, can we deal with your general comments? What was your conclusion, please, in relation to the JNA involvement in this convoy and --

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: "My conclusion is, from the JNA, that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Evacuation?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- there were very bad organisation in the evacuation, in logistic, organisation, work, and priority, and they were good organised in the infirmary and there were no security of the wounded and there were some drunk officers, there were no control over the Chetnik, and they removed wounded and staff before ICMM arrived. And they were shooting mortar from Vukovar."

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And then we've got the ICRC, which perhaps I needn't repeat as it was a summary?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was bad leader and -- the leader was bad and there were no help the 20th of November, but good help in 21 of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'd like to move on to another topic if I may, please. You were asked by counsel on behalf of Mr. Sljivancanin about what I will call the evacuation agreement -- agreement, and I would like you to turn up, please, to our Exhibit 40, at tab 20. And you were asked questions about manning or personnel to help the evacuation. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, can we please look at the agreement a little more carefully? Can we please look at paragraph 4? Have you got that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Shall I read it to assist? "The YPA will provide suitable military vehicles for the movement from Vukovar to Zidine, and the Republic of Croatia will provide suitable vehicles for the remainder of the journey." The next part, please. "Both parties will provide suitably equipped and manned ambulances for some 40 seriously ill and lorries and coaches." Can you explain to me how it was that you said that there was no mention of personnel in this agreement when we have the reference to "manned"? Can you just explain to me and to the Court?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the answer -- the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You seem to suggest that there was nothing in the agreement about manned. Manned means personnel?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Manned means personnel, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And you said there was nothing in the agreement about that. Having looked at this, does this assist you in any way?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when there's mentioned here, manned ambulances, there must be some you can say hospital personnel any kind, military or civilian, in the ambulance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And does that apply as we read on to lorries and coaches as well? Presuming that they don't drive themselves?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there must be some staff, some men, some hospital staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. Can I just move on to another piece of evidence that you -- you gave, it relates to the 18th, I think the 18th of November. I believe it's November. And you were asked as a result of questions by Mr. Bulatovic, you came to the conclusion that the hospital was under the control of the ZNG. Can I just try and clarify that, please? On the 18th of October [sic] did you actually go to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 18th, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Then if you didn't go to the hospital, how do you know it was under the control of the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the -- by the -- just a moment. We were told by the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So in actual fact you didn't have any personal knowledge yourself; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I just go through with one or two other points, please? Dealing with weapons. You have a military background, you had a military background in 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: You were asked by the Danish military to assess the weapons that perhaps were unsure around Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not special around Vukovar, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Was Vukovar part of that brief?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So you weren't to look at any of the weapons around Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were looking after weapon all over Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, line 29:25, I think it was the 18th of November, not October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I thought I said November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you did. I'm pointing it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal then, please, can we focus on military weapons around the Vukovar area. You were there the 18th, 19th and 20th, and 21st, actually. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, can we deal with the -- with the weapons that you saw and what I will call the JNA saw and weapons that you saw on what I will call the Croatian side for -- for assistance? Now, can I deal with the JNA side?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because -- you can -- you can deal with JNA because I saw no Croatian soldiers on the 18th, 19th, 20th, and 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But I want to deal with weapons. Things like tanks, artillery, multiple-rocket launchers. Did you see any tanks around Vukovar on any of those days?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the sort of tanks, the number of tanks, can you tell us about the JNA side compared by the Croat side? Numbers, for example?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry for interrupting. The witness was quite clear about not seeing any Croatian forces on the 18th, 19th, and 20th. If he saw no Croatian forces, then how can he be expected to speak about any weapons they had, including heavy weapons? I believe the question is somewhat too leading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would submit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Borovic, I don't see the question to be leading when it's asking about specific types of armament. And in truth if none was seen is the answer, then we can move on quickly. Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're quite right, Your Honour, I accept that, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you see any multiple rocket launchers?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw one, I think it was the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And are you able to tell us, it was on the JNA side or Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the JNA side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And with regard to the multiple-rocket launcher, there are various sorts, there are ones on large lorries and there are ones that can be towed. Can you remember in general terms, the sort size of it?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember it was an - what do you call it? - a small-size one who had to be collect up by another vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Now, can you help me please from your own military experience, if you have a military -- if you have a mobile rocket launcher, what is the nature of that weapon when it actually fires items? Does it deal with a specific target precisely, or is it an -- an item that deals with an area?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It deals with an area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Can we deal with artillery? Did you see any artillery pieces?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about tanks?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw tanks, I think it was just outside Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Did you see any Croatian tanks?

utterances.speaker: JAN SCHOU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see any Croatian forces at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour forgive me a moment? I just may have one more question. I have no more questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Moore. Dr. Schou, you will be pleased to know that that is the end of your questioning. The Chamber would like to thank you for your attendance here in The Hague, and for the assistance you have been able to give. And you may of course now return to your home and other responsibilities. Thank you, indeed. We must now have the first break and will resume at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we ask for 10 more minutes than that? And may I explain why? We were given a large bundle by Dr. Bosanac last week. We have had a photocopied. And quite simply we've given it to my learned friends. We have other bundles as well. We are trying to highlight them in a way that will assist everybody and to put them into files. You have probably seen people coming in and out of court. And if I could perhaps have an extra 10 minutes I would then hope that the documents would be then be able available for everybody and I believe it will speed up the proceedings this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well, but you may be able to help me. I raised on Friday the diary, or notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I am told that they have not been --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Apparently not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- tendered yet. Do you propose to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, I make application for the original diary and for the typed translation to accompany it. Perhaps the diary can be A, and the translation can be B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received, both part of the same exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the diary will be Exhibit Number 344.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will resume at a quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I hope that was time enough for your needs, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It was, thank you very much. And I am very grateful. Can I just indicate, because my learned friends and I agreed to keep the witness out pro tem, the situation with Dr. Bosanac, who is being recalled, is as follows: In September, October, she provided a CD which I did mention to the Court when she was called, and that has been downloaded and is in hard copy. The problem that we had with that document was it mentioned all the people who had been at the hospital for the year, I think, 1991. We had other dates as well. Because of the concern over medical privilege the names were redacted, but all the other details were disclosed. That document is now in hard copy form, and I've got it for the Court. May I just pass this forward at this time so that I can explain certain matters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And the Defence have got it as well. The document that the Court has with the blue file has got -- it's an OTP document, if I may use that phrase. There is an index which is fairly straightforward, and then if one goes to the first page one can see that there would have been names and if, for example, one just casually flicks through the document, you can see occasionally names on the left-hand side. The best example of it, I suppose, would be page 29 where we can see five names. I only choose that page for -- for assistance. Now, those names that are there are individuals who were at the Vukovar Hospital as we would submit, and who subsequently, again, we submit, were killed at Ovcara. So it links with the appendix on the indictment. One can see that in actual fact there is a burgundy colour. The index shows quite clearly that there is a slight discrepancy in spelling and I can deal with that in due course. With regard to the yellow, there is a discrepancy with date of birth. And then there is the three other heads, which are in black, green, and blue. That is the OTP document. Could I just indicate how it came to fruition, again to assist the Court. When we supplied the Defence with the CD, we then printed in hard copy. And this is the document. It is an enormous document. My learned friends have got it. And what I have attempted to do is extract from this document the relevant parts. Namely, the name of the person, if they were deceased, the date of admission, the location where they came from, and the diagnosis of injury. And whether in actual fact they were part of ZNG or any other element, I've tried to encapsulate all the points that would assist my learned friend, the Court and my learned friends, not only to myself in evidence-in-chief, but also in cross-examination. So this is an extraction from the large document, the blue is the extraction from the large document. I have not printed up the large document because it's almost unintelligible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, can you tell me, most spaces for the name are blank?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, they are individuals who, we submit, are still living. They are people who were entered into the Vukovar Hospital at some time. If I take the first page by way of example -- just get my glasses. One can see, and I hope that I get it right, that it's blank, then we've got ZNG, so that person was entered as a member of the ZNG, the date of entry to the hospital, as far as I'm aware, is the 17th of the 10th. Then it is the location where they came from is Vukovar, we have a diagnosis of the injury. I believe that the -- the Datum Unosa is the date of entry. Because this document, if I just forewarn the court and my learned friends, was created by the hospital, I would submit the evidence will be as follows: That the details were -- a patient would come in, they would be registered. The registration details would then be e-mailed or sent to Zagreb. And the -- this document, or the large document, was created as a result of the compiling of the information in Zagreb. And then it has been given back to the hospital. There were no records at the hospital, because you may remember that Dr. Bosanac said that the records were taken away after the fall of the hospital, and they have never been recovered. So this is a document which has been compiled as a result of registration, then transmission to Zagreb, and the document then coming back and Dr. Bosanac saying, as I believe she will, that this document correctly encapsulates or records the people in the hospital. So that is the blue document. The second document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The named people then are those who are dead?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: On your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. And they will link, I believe, with -- if one looks metaphorically into the -- the appendix to the indictment there are names there. And those names can be found, where appropriate, can be found on the left-hand side. So, for example, as I say, if I take the first example, there is none on page 1, page 3, 3 has got one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is enough for us to know that that is a person whom you advance as dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What about those who are missing?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: There is a different document which was being brought by Dr. Bosanac which is the document that I have in front of me, this very large document. And the way that that appears to have been constructed is that there are three subdivisions. Subdivision A is a group of people by Dr. Bosanac's counting, 97 of those people are named in the annex to the indictment that she indicated that they are wounded, and they were in the Vukovar Hospital at the time of the fall of Vukovar. There are -- so you are talking about 97 of them, there are three spelling irregularities and two that are actually not named in the indictment and they are located -- or they were exhumed at Ovcara and we will hear evidence subsequently identified by Guncevic -- Grujic, my apologies. So with regard to that list, it comes from the hospital, they are named in the indictment, they are wounded, and they are exhumed at Ovcara, and identified by one of two methods. So that's one of the subdivisions. The second subdivision relates again to people who were exhumed at Ovcara, they are named in the annex of the indictment, they are identified by Grujic and those again are people that Dr. Bosanac says were at the hospital, but are not on the large list as wounded. So you have one that's wounded, one that's not. The third category that Your Honour has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: 97 in the first category. And in the second?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think it's 94. I'll just check, if I may. There are 96 victims identified at Ovcara that are on the hospital list. 92 of those were identified at Ovcara that are not on the hospital list. Then with regard to the second list that I have from Dr. Bosanac, there are 94. So with regard to the ones that are not on the wounded list, there are 94. With regard to the first, I believe there are 97. And then with regard to the third list and the one that Your Honour has referred to, these are 45 people that are recorded as being present, wounded or not, but they are still missing. And 34 of those are in the indictment. So it's rather complicated and I'm sorry if I'm not making it clear, but with regard to the -- the way it has been done is that there has been a database created with people who are wounded at the Vukovar Hospital, we have extracted those people, we have tried to link them with the Ovcara victims, and the method of identification coming from the hospital and the ones who are not on the record but nevertheless through whatever means it might be identification visually, it might be through knowledge, it might be through hearsay, there is a group there. And then finally there is a group of people who are not -- who are recorded as being present but are still missing so there is no evidence of -- of death. I give the best example, which is Martin Dosen. Martin Dosen, there is evidence clearly that he was at the hospital, there is evidence of behaviour at the JNA barracks. He is on the indictment as being a victim, but his remains have been never discovered. So there is no evidence actually that -- that he was killed. But we will obviously submit that the inference is that he was. But that's in for example that third category. So what I want to do, with the Court's leave, and I'm sorry to take a little bit of time is to call Dr. Bosanac to explain the methodology of compiling the names, how it -- the list was created, then move on to the large list that she brought last week, and then there is the subsidiary point of the documents, two documents that she has to be cross-examined on. I tried to bring it down into as tight a piece of evidence as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore. So are you ready to recall the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I'm ready to start and I hope that everything will be intelligible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't like the Prosecutor to start examining the witness before we explain our position concerning these documents. On behalf of our Defence team and I believe my other colleagues support me as well, I would like to say two things. I believe that the Chamber should be familiar with these two issues. As to how we are going to cross-examine the witness concerning these documents. In relation to the first document mentioned by Mr. Moore, the database in the blue folder that Mrs. Bosanac is to give us some explanation about, I have to tell you the following: We received, I believe, binder 78, from the Prosecution on the 13th of December, 2005. We received the document, or that is to say the lists that we have now before us, but without a single name entered into it. It was only five minutes ago, just before the Chamber entered the courtroom, that we received the document with the names of certain persons. We were unable to go through it physically. Before that we had a document without a single name. This created certain problems for us concerning the cross-examination of the witness on this document. What Mr. Moore said now, and what in my view represents something that can be a starting point for all of us in this courtroom, is this: If this document is a database, if this reflects the data sent from the Vukovar Hospital to the Ministry of Health in Zagreb, then it is necessary for the Defence to be given the documents based on which this database was created. Not a single document from the Ministry of Health or from Dr. Bosanac was received by us in order to explain how the database was created. Therefore, how can we be expected to cross-examine the witness when we do not know how this document was compiled? Another issue that concerns me even more is the second document. Document containing 97 names. And I will explain why it concerns me. When I cross-examined Mrs. Bosanac on the 31st of October she said then for the first time that she had with her the document containing the names of 97 wound persons, as she described them, from the Vukovar Hospital. When Mr. Moore, on page 892, conducted redirect examination, this is what was recorded in the transcript. I will read this out now. [In English] Page 892, 31st of October, line 19:

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: "You were asked by my learned friend Mr. Lukic about various list and numbers and you replied that you had a list of 97 people who were registered and wounded and subsequently killed in Ovcara. Do you still have that list, or do you have that list with you now?" Answer: "I still have it." Question: "Do you have it in court with you?" Answer: "Yes." [Interpretation] Mr. Moore said to us on Thursday that he received the document from Mrs. Bosanac when she came back here again. We found these documents in our lockers on Friday when we came to the Tribunal. Something that was said by Mrs. Bosanac three months ago was given to us three days ago. It wouldn't be too unusual, but once my colleagues and I went through these -- through this document we realised that certain data had been entered into the document that can be of great relevance, both for the Prosecution and the Defence. Status of the persons is mentioned in these documents. Then there is a general description of injuries. And then in relation to the other lists containing 94 persons who were not wounded, it also defined their status as combatants. Now, after we have heard all Croatian witnesses, members of the ZNG and hospital staff, we are now being given this document when we no longer have the opportunity to examine them about those who were admitted into the hospital or those who were not wounded but came to the hospital nevertheless, those 18 -- on the 18th. This is very important for the Defence case, namely the status that the persons had on the 20th in the morning when they were taken to the barracks. Now we have no one to ask anyone, we have no one to examine on the status of certain persons and we could have been given this information back on the 31st of October, or the 1st of November, because this is what the witness said in the courtroom. Let me give you an example. Polovina Branimir is mentioned. He is the late husband of witness Zvezdana Polovina, and in this document it says he was a defender. We did not have this information when we cross-examined Mrs. Polovina. We only have his evidence and what she said about him working for Radio Vukovar. Therefore we are now taken aback by this situation. We found ourselves in a very complicated situation because we not only have to cross-examine Mrs. Bosanac on this issue, but we are also unable to examine a large number of witnesses who could have told us relevant information about the status of these persons. Perhaps I took too long to explain this, and perhaps I wasn't too clear, but this is a very important issue for our Defence. If you need us to clarify this further, we are ready to do so. I just wanted to make you aware of this before Mrs. Bosanac entered the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, what is it that you propose?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am now taken by surprise by your question. I should have expected it though. Let me suggest the following: We can examine Mrs. Bosanac about these documents and then we can ask the Prosecution to provide the source that was used to compile this document reflecting the information that was accident from the hospital to the Ministry of Health. As for the document containing 97 names, where there is some description of injuries, we need to verify this information and for that we need the assistance of our experts. And should we find something that is important for the remaining 94 persons, then we would perhaps ask the courtroom to bring back some witnesses. We do not wish to take this course of action though. I believe that this should have been provided to us at a much earlier stage when we still had the chance to examine witnesses on these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: We provided to my learned friend the list in CD form with the names redacted. That was three and a half months ago. Within the list there are the actual specified occupations. Whether it's ZNG, whether they're civilians. So my learned friends have got that material and have had it since December. If there is concern about a particular witness, for my part I have never been asked whether there was any document in support of it. All I can say is that in relation to this document, which I have compiled over the weekend because of the arrival of the new document, the names have been inserted to try and help all parties. The status can be established by, I'm quite sure, admission. If my learned friends want me to admit that somebody is a member of the ZNG or that he's a member of the civil defence, and it's shown on the hospital register, then I will do so. I have no problems about that at all. The only concern that I have ever had, and it was communicated by Dr. Bosanac, was that she had been given that material through medical confidentiality, and she instructed me, or OTP that she did not want the names and did not wish to release the names of people who were living and perhaps were on this list as members of the ZNG. Now, if my learned friend wishes that fact to be revealed, then he can make an application to the Court for that redaction to be removed. But as matters stand, we are caught in the middle. This is the hospital saying this is confidential material, and we do not wish it to be disclosed. If they want it disclosed, they can make an application for it to be disclosed. That is the position. And with regard to the new material suddenly appearing, this material is almost the same as the material that came on Thursday. The material that came on Thursday is almost like a bibliography, which has got sources, three or four sources. Whether the Court paid considerable attention to it is a matter for the Court, but it may not be of tremendous assistance to the Court but nevertheless it has been served on me and I have served it to the Defence. So that is all we have done. So if my learned friend says they wanted to cross-examine about such and such a person being a member of the ZNG if he mentions this name, it is on this list, I will admit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore another matter raised as I understood it, by Mr. Lukic, is the source documents for the preparation in Zagreb of this list. In other words, what was transmitted from the hospital. Have they been discovered or disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The source documents, if I may put it this way: There are really two sources. The initial source, as far as I understand it, comes from the hospital. And the records of the hospital were destroyed or should I say taken away, either the 20th or the 21st of November. There is no documentary source material in the presence -- or under the control of the OTP. My understanding is that Dr. Bosanac will say that she sent the material on a day-by-day basis to Zagreb for the compilation of list and she then subsequently got back the various names and the details that she had provided, but back in a form that is -- the Court has already seen. And, as I say, it is in this particular form, the way it came back. And this is exactly what the Defence have had since December. So if there was so much concern, I'm rather surprised there hasn't been an application before now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Lukic, where does that put you and other Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the question you asked Mr. Moore was the right one. And that is the essence of the entire matter. Even while cross-examining Ms. Bosanac I asked her, the reports that you kept sending to Zagreb on a daily basis, did you see those only after you had arrived in Zagreb and she said, some yes and some no.
