This is the basic issue around which everything revolved. What was the table containing this information based on. We can proceed from there. If Ms. Bosanac is concerned about the secrecy of these documents, I don't think that should be too difficult to deal with. We can go into closed session. We can tender them under seal. But it is very difficult for us to know what the source is for these lists. It's what I believe she had been sending up until the 6th of November by e-mail, but then she continued up until the 17th of November on a daily basis, these reports. And we haven't seen a single one in the courtroom. And I don't suppose that the OTP have either. I think it would be necessary to have these, because this is the only possible foundation for our cross-examination that I am able to imagine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I don't understand it to be advanced that there is any secrecy issue. The professional confidentiality issue is raised in respect of individual names. If that is an issue for any particular person, I would take it Defence counsel are able to refer that to Mr. Moore, and he can tell you one that is in these lists. Is that -- is there a problem with that that anybody sees?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is not a problem when speaking about specific persons. But what is of paramount importance to us is to see the source on which this document was based. As for the reports, we realise that any medical files are confidential and secret, if you like. I remember that being the case the last time we discussed these documents, specifically with Ms. Dosen. But it's very difficult for us to verify the authenticity of this information if we don't know where it came from. We've seen all the appeals by Ms. Bosanac about the number of patients. I assume that this was more or less the substance of her daily reports as well. Maybe the names are not there at all. Maybe what is there is just the figures and the descriptions of their injuries. I don't think Mr. Moore knows either. But then I am entitled to ask myself and everyone else, what the purpose is, potentially, of our cross-examination, since we don't know the very first thing, and that is what this document was based on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, we haven't heard Dr. Bosanac, but Dr. Bosanac, I will ask her exactly the procedure for registration, what she then did with that -- that information, where it went.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The issue is the documents that were transmitted by one means or another to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are they available or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I don't have them. I've never seen them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That doesn't answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, it doesn't, but I can't answer the question, I can only answer that which I know, and that is I haven't seen them. I can certainly make inquiries if the Court would wish me to do so. In any event, and I do accept that, because it obviously goes to the weight reliability of the document, I understand that. But nevertheless it does not preclude the doctor from giving evidence, in my submission, about seeing the various names in this particular document, and whether it accords with her recollection. I'm not saying she remembers 1.000 patients, that would be ridiculous, but whether it accords with her recollection of certain individuals, what the diagnosis was and the dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There is no issue at the moment of admissibility. The issue is -- you say it goes to weight. It also goes to fairness of trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the question that is exercising the Chamber is whether it's convenient to proceed with the doctor's evidence before these documents, if they exist are provided. Because if cross-examination is going to focus on them, they need to be available and study -- be studied before cross-examination occurred. Now, if they're not available, they don't exist, we have a different lot of issues. And weight is the centre of that. But while we're looking at fairness of trial --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- if these are produced from source documents, the issue is whether they are available or not, and whether the trial can proceed fairly with them not being made available to the Defence. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I do. Might I submit it's really a two-part question. The first part is, can Dr. Bosanac give evidence fairly and appropriately of the method of collation of the material and the transmission of the material to Zagreb. Part B of that part is when the documentation comes back from Zagreb, whether she independently is able to confirm whether those names and details correspond with her recollection of what she sent off. That's the first part. The second part is -- relates to how the material was treated and compiled in Zagreb. I have the answer in relation to part one; I do not have the answer in relation to part two. And I would merely submit, and beg the question, how can Dr. Bosanac be cross-examined on the collation of the Zagreb material if she played no part in it. So therefore I think it would be fair for her to give evidence on the first part, namely the registration and transmission of the material, what she knows about, and then quite simply the second part can be dealt with, if needs be, either by a new witness, or the Court to say quite simply, we have -- move on in time, I have heard Dr. Bosanac's evidence; however, there is a missing people, namely the collation of the Zagreb -- or how it was done in Zagreb, and therefore we are not satisfied with the reliability of the evidence and it shouldn't be considered. But these are two parts. And Bosanac could not be cross-examined logically and sensibly on what happened in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: She could be cross-examined on the content of what she transmitted --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- as revealed by the original documents. And what appears this these secondary documents, if they differ. The question is whether they differ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac can be cross-examined, clearly, about how the document -- sorry. How witnesses or how persons coming to the hospital, how they were registered, what sort of details were put in. Because for example, there may be various hallmarks of material which would then and could be used by the Court to establish whether the Zagreb collation was accurate or not. But Bosanac can be cross-examined on what happened in relation to the Vukovar Hospital and Bosanac can be cross-examined if needs be about what happened to the original source documents. There is nothing, in my submission, to stop that. But accept entirely what my learned friend says about the Zagreb link, and she cannot be cross-examined about that, because there is nothing she can add about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You have repeated your earlier submission, I won't bother repeating my reply comment to you, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May I deal with the second document, if it helps? The large document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Again, that document that was brought last week, my understanding is that the source of the document, the source material, is various. It can be, for example, the widows of Vukovar or some interested group. So it may well be the Court would think it is not a particularly helpful document. It does not go to Zagreb, although I think Zagreb may play a part in it. But again, Dr. Bosanac can be cross-examined on the creation of that material, but cannot be cross-examined in relation to other material of which she is unaware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: One further question. Are you saying that Dr. Bosanac will be able to give evidence that the material she transmitted to Zagreb did not return to the hospital, but what returned was documents in the form that you have there and have been disclosed to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And that that occurred in all cases that are to be in the documents that are exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour forgive me one moment? I missed something. Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Moore. Anything further, Mr. Lukic? I take it you are speaking for all three Defence teams? Yes. Yes, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Just to assist about the accompanying documents in relation to this last document. I think the Chamber would probably be very interested in seeing all these other documents or medical documents, or how these persons were diagnosed, in what way. If we keep in mind the fact that some were shamming wounds, a lot of questions can be asked about how they were diagnosed. And how is that consistent with some of the testimony that we heard in this case? What my learned friend, Mr. Lukic, said about the documents that were sent to Zagreb, I believe the same applies to the medical files which should perhaps have been used to corroborate this other document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The problem with that, Mr. Borovic, is the evidence that all the medical files do not now exist. They were removed from the hospital by the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do not wish to argue with you. Some were removed and some were perhaps not. I'm sure that many of the documents were kept by the patients themselves. It also remains to check the authenticity of all the wounds in relation to all the persons whose names are on the list. These are facts to be verified. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. I fully agree with everything that my learned friends have been saying. But there are two issues that I would like to draw the Chamber's attention to, which I think are important. Firstly, if we look at the blue file at the reports, that have kindly been served on us by my learned friend, it is obvious that the diagnosis is there for each of the patients. It is understandable for the Defence to ask questions about how these were obtained if Croatia's health ministry had no access to any medical files. That is precisely why we would like to know more about the source documents based on which Croatia's health ministry compiled an overview like this, or a list like this. Providing the exact diagnosis in relation to each and every patient on the list, or at least that's what they came. These reports must exist somewhere. Perhaps the witness, Dr. Bosanac, could help us out with this and disclose the whereabouts of these documents if by any chance she knows. Secondly, I would like to comment on what my learned friend has mentioned. The fact that the Defence were informed of these documents in the blue file back in December. What I would like to point out is that we did indeed receive a CD containing these documents back in December, but as my learned friend, Mr. Lukic, said, without a single name. Which begs the question, what could the Defence possibly have checked for authenticity if we didn't know who the persons were to begin with? This is just useless information without the names of these persons. We are supposed to be checking whether these persons were really wounded, whether these persons were in the hospital on the 18th, 19th or 20th of November. Whether these persons' ailments really was consistent with their respective diagnoses stated here. And finally whether these persons were taken away from the hospital and taken to Ovcara. We have not been able to resolve any of these important questions because we didn't have a single name to go on. I'm slightly surprised by the concern expressed by my learned friend in relation to the confidential nature of these documents, at least as they relate to people who are still alive. We, the Defence teams, have no intention on insisting on such documents, because they are no part of the indictment, but we do have the right to insist to be given information in relation to all those people whose names are in the annex to our indictment and who the OTP claims were taken away from the Vukovar Hospital. In actual fact, only now, only today, are we truly in a position to tackle these issues and to verify this information; only now do we have the names. As concerns the documents in relation to the 97 persons, which my learned friend has mentioned, there is one thing I would like to say. I think these documents too, were obtained from the medical headquarters of Croatia's health ministry, at least that's what the heading suggests. Which is to say these documents too were derived from earlier documents which should exist somewhere and which had to come from the Vukovar Hospital at some point. Each and every person mentioned in this report has a diagnosis, an abbreviated one, but different from the one specified in the so-called blue file. At least that's what a cursory glance seems to suggest. In the sense that the one in the blue file is either not as comprehensive or not as accurate, therefore I believe what has been pointed out by my learned friend, Mr. Lukic, as being a problem that the Defence has encountered in terms of obligations under Article 21, item 4 of the Statute, the fact is that we must be given a chance to study the documents on which the reports that my learned friend has mentioned are based. It is true that we did not have an opportunity to cross-examine many of the witnesses on these individuals whose names are mentioned here, but what that means is that the Defence should have a chance to deal with all the names, and to try and at least check the essentials. Were these persons wounded persons, were these persons at the hospital at the time, and were they, in fact, taken away from the hospital at the time relevant to what we are talking about. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, do I understand from you that you now have the names of all those who were in these lists who are also in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, unfortunately I can't provide a perfectly accurate answer. We were just given these documents today and we have not had a chance to check any of it. What a cursory glance would reveal is that some names are mentioned, as my learned friend from the OTP has said. Some names on the indictment are there, but I am unable to tell you at this point in time that all of the names are there. For the simple reason that the Defence teams have not had a chance to go through all these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The further question I have for you, Mr. Vasic, is the Chamber correct in understanding that there has been no application to lift redactions on the information that you were provided in December, and there has been no motion about the disclosure of the documents that were sent to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, bearing in mind the results of Mrs. Bosanac's examination-in-chief and cross-examination which occurred in October and November, as my learned friend Mr. Lukic has mentioned, and bearing in mind the fact that my learned friend Mr. Moore said at the time that he was in possession of documents, but there was a confidentiality issue attached to these documents, and he didn't know at the time in what way and to what extent he would be using these documents. Given all of that, I don't think the Defence was in a position to foresee that these documents would be used in the way that they are being used now. At any rate, if under Rule 66(A)(ii), that was the intention of OTP, a full list of names and documents bearing all the names should have been served on the Defence. I think that much is certain. There was no way for us to know whether certain persons from the list, the list that we were given on a CD, are alive or dead. Missing or not missing, because that is just not information included in this list. I think it was the duty of the OTP, if they were ever going to use the document in this way, to inform the Defence of its substance in a timely manner. And to specify which persons were missing and which person where is not, as well as to provide their names so that we would have a chance to check all this information in a timely manner. Just in order to answer your question, the Defence have not asked the OTP to lift the secretly ruling for -- in relation to some of the names for this very reason. We simply didn't know who the people were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Surely, Mr. Vasic, instead of focusing on whether there had been a full disclosure to you, there having been a redacted disclosure, if you were pursuing the question of the medical condition and genuineness of the alleged injuries of those named in the indictment who were contained in the information disclosed to you, and you found that you couldn't examine that issue because the names were redacted, that it would have been self-evident that you should have got an order to lift the redactions so that you could pursue the question which each counsel for the Defence now stresses to us is so important. How genuine were these injuries, what were they, how reliably were they diagnosed, et cetera, in respect of those who are alleged in the indictment to have been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the document that we were given contained no information to show the Defence who the persons were. Or indeed that those were the same persons as those mentioned in the annex to the indictment. Not even generally speaking. Another thing that was being discussed at the time was the possibility of Mr. Moore using this document. Let me remind you this is not an original hospital document. This is a collection compiled by the health ministry. Therefore, back in December there was no way we could ever imagine that this document would be used by the OTP as a document that would again resurface during the additional examination of Dr. Bosanac. However, I think the onus is on the OTP to inform the Defence of all these details in a timely manner, especially in view of the fact that we are dealing here with a document that is not an original document. This is something that was compiled based on a number of other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. Is there anything further, Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Just very briefly, yes. In December Dr. Bosanac, it was -- there was an agreement that she was to be recalled to be cross-examined on this document. She wasn't being recalled because of two later documents that were discovered, she was being recalled because of this document itself. That was the first point. So it's not right for my learned friends -- the transcript can be checked in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I have it here, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I hope I'm right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. And the second point is this: That this case is -- deals principally with the removal of persons from the hospital, some of whom were injured. That was in -- in the opening and it's in the evidence. Now, what on earth did my learned friends think that the purpose of the document was for, if not to demonstrate that some of the people who were subsequently exhumed at Ovcara came from the hospital and were undergoing medical treatment? And, thirdly, although Your Honour has dealt with it, we have never had any application to say that the Defence were disadvantaged because they don't have access to the names. So those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think I can just see you, Mr. Lukic. I think we've done submissions just about to their end. But, yes, you've got one last quick say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be very brief, Your Honour. Let me just repeat this: The first document from the blue file, let me say, was served on us in December. It was then that Mr. Moore told us that he was unable at the time to give us the names for reasons of confidentiality. That was the reason that we never decided to even try to ascertain the identity of the persons from that list. What we did expect Mr. Moore to do, and this is clear if you look at the transcript dated the 31st of October, was to give us the sources that Dr. Bosanac used for this report. I have a suspicion you are about to tell me that I'm wrong, but based on the 31st of October and the relevant transcript, I was expecting that Dr. Bosanac would be examined on those documents, and we wanted to examine her on Rule 68 documents, at least that was my reading of the 31st of October transcript. And if my reading of the transcript was erroneous, I am sure you are about to tell me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did you mean October? I'm looking at a transcript, of the 31st of January this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was looking at the transcript dated the 31st of October when we concluded the examination of Mrs. Bosanac, and when the problem with this document arose. That was the transcript that I looked at, and not the one that you just mentioned. My case manager is now telling me that on the 24th of January we discussed about the documents disclosed pursuant to Rule 68, and it was then that we submitted a motion to have Dr. Bosanac recalled, and I guess that your decision then pertained to this request put it on the 24th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's it. 31st of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, there seem to be questions about -- unresolved about the availability today of the documents transmitted from the hospital to Zagreb upon which at least the most critical component of these -- your blue folder --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- is based.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: For the purposes of cross-examination, if they are available, those source documents, in respect of the persons alleged in the indictment now to be dead it would seem that they should be made available to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If there is uncertainty in your mind about their availability which can be resolved by getting instructions from Dr. Bosanac, we could adjourn now to enable you to get those instructions during the break. If there is any other issue relating to these documents about which you could receive further information from Dr. Bosanac before her evidence commences --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- that again could be dealt with in an adjournment now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you believe you are adequately informed on those matters and want to proceed with her evidence in chief now, that can occur. Although of course there will need to be a break in a relatively short time. Whether or not at the end of her evidence, if it is your decision to proceed with her now, that there is need for some adjournment to allow the Defence to cope with this new information, then that will be an issue that would have to be dealt with at the end of the evidence in chief. At the moment there is too little known for us to reach any final decision about it. So, essentially her -- the evidence of the doctor can proceed now, her evidence in chief. If you want to take further instructions from her before commencing her evidence, we would allow an adjournment to enable to you do that. The other course is whether you want to simply defer Dr. Bosanac altogether rather than have the prospect of her giving evidence in yet two further bites rather than one. We could consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, might I accept the Court's invitation to have the adjournment now? I will speak to Dr. Bosanac, because obviously there are two questions: One, about her state of knowledge, and two, about her availability. So if I can be permitted to speak to her, as you have requested, I will do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. And I trust the Defence will understand from that that the doctor well now be called to give her evidence in chief. At the end of her evidence in chief, if there are still significant issues of difficulty, that can be heard again and the matter ruled upon. Very well. Unfortunately then we must now adjourn. Would 20 minutes be enough, Mr. Moore, or do you want 30 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, I would think 20 minutes would be adequate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will resume at 10 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have been able to speak to Dr. Bosanac. Might I submit or make a suggestion? Dr. Bosanac, when I inquired about the source material, basically repeat that had which I have already said to the Court, and I'm not going to repeat. However, she believes that the original source material may be held in Zagreb. For my part, the reason that she thinks that is if a person for example has hurt their leg, she had an example of that recently, that they would come and then contact Zagreb, and Zagreb would confirm that that person was at the Vukovar Hospital and had a damaged leg, and I presume a pension. But that is capable, that decision is capable of coming from the -- the collated information as much as the original source material. What I would submit as an appropriate course would be as follows: For -- we are in court tomorrow afternoon at 2.15. For Dr. Bosanac at 9.00 tomorrow morning to contact Zagreb. She knows the departments and she knows the people who allegedly deal with this material and would be able to ascertain quicker than any investigator would whether in actual fact the material is available, or whether it is in collated form. Now, if Dr. Bosanac starts her evidence in chief, which I am prepared to start, it creates somewhat of a difficulty in the sense that she is a witness giving evidence and I am not able to talk to her really in that she would be in the middle of giving evidence and I would be asking discussions with her. If she doesn't start then I can sit with her and try and ascertain actually what is required and what is needed. And if the material is not therefore available, then we know exactly where we stand. We do have Dr. Njavro, and we can proceed with Dr. Njavro, although Dr. Bosanac herself says that she would not like to come back a third time for obvious reasons. But the situation is we can proceed with Dr. Njavro, if things aren't ready to proceed. And we would be able to contact the office of OTP in Zagreb to try and locate, or bring the documents to The Hague, if needs be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So your proposal is that we should adjourn today?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And resume tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, or earlier if the Court want. And I will deal with Dr. Njavro [sic] tomorrow morning and try and find out exactly whether this source material is available or whether it is now being put into collated form, and maybe I can ascertain who did and perhaps he can call evidence to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You probably meant Dr. Bosanac. Not Njavro.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's my submission, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think, in view of the significance of this issue for the Defence, that is the appropriate course to take, regrettably. So I am afraid we must adjourn now to resume tomorrow at 2.15 we're in, I believe, number 1 court tomorrow, not this court. We will now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 4th day of April, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.00 p.m.,
